doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Quitting in L.A. and choosing the West Coast
summary: He quit when the song became a hit, stayed in California, and loved the space, openness and mix of music in the sixties.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Because it was like — rickey tickey. Well it becomes a hit and we’re playing it every night. You know and my wife was pregnant at the time and we were in L.A., and I said we couldn’t go back she was having a baby any minute so I said well I’m quitting. So I quit in L.A. And we stayed out here. We had the baby, we were in L.A. and I just never went back to the East Coast. I mean I go back and everything but I just — it was just a different world. First it was a lot of space and I grew up back east and I felt really, I could really breathe out here. And I really liked the temperament of the people. I thought the people were a lot more open on the West Coast than they were here, so a lot of different things. And it was the sixties, so you know it was, it was just like pretty wild. I mean you had the heavyweight black politics on one side, you have the hippies over here burning down Berkeley — really — all this different flow of music that was happening, a real strong Latino thing. I never knew any Latino people on the East Coast, not really.

No I was just totally on a bebop thing and out here I met people — you know Asians playing jazz, and playing their own music. It really opened my eyes. I just really — and plus I could hike. I could get out, I could just drive fifty miles and be in the wilderness. And that’s still one of the things that I can’t wait — even when I go anywhere I can’t wait to get back here, the little secret places I go, I’ve got my kayak. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
I’ve got my grandsons who love to fish. What more could I ask for?
And I have a new set of Sonar drums.
It looks like you’re in the pink.
